## Summary

When the Soviet Union ended, prices had been fixed for decades while savings and money piled up with nothing to buy. On **2 January 1992**, Russia lifted most price controls. Prices jumped **245 % in January 1992** (H&K; doubling every 17.0 days), and that single month is the whole hyperinflation by the 50 % definition. But inflation stayed in the thousands of percent for the year, about **2,500 % in 1992**, and the ruble kept falling until "Black Tuesday" in October 1994.

## Causes

- **A monetary overhang.** Under fixed Soviet prices, households and firms had piled up roubles they
  could not spend. Freeing prices released that pile all at once.

## Timeline

- **2 Jan 1992** — "shock therapy" begins under Yegor Gaidar: most prices are freed.
- **Jan 1992** — prices rise 245 % in the month (H&K). Wikipedia reports "300 %", and about
  1,000 % in the first quarter.
- **1992** — 2,509 % for the year.
- **11 Oct 1994** — Black Tuesday, the ruble crash.
- **1998** — redenomination at 1,000 : 1, on the brink of the August 1998 crisis (Wikipedia, Russian ruble).

## Lessons

- Freeing prices does not create inflation, it shows inflation that was already there: the
  repressed overhang appears in one month.
- One month above 50 % makes it a hyperinflation on paper. What ruined savers was the three years
  of high inflation that followed.
